addresses_holes: c11 H1 (≤30% ceiling cascades to 3-4 stations)
patches.find: Across the 2026-08-12 station set, most stations sit inside the 30°–50° CGM band. The binary classifier therefore predicts an approximately constant amplitude for the European core, with only LER (≳58° CGM) clearly outside. That yields 2–3 unique predicted values across nine stations
patches.replace: Across the 2026-08-12 station set the CGM-band membership is sharper than the wins.json text previously stated. Centered-dipole computation with IGRF-14 epoch 2020 pole (80.65°N, 287.32°E) gives station CGM latitudes: COI 43.7°, EBR 42.9°, SPT 42.4°, CLF 49.6° — all clearly inside the 30°–50° band; SNK 33.2° — inside, low-latitude edge; NGK 51.85° — sitting on the upper boundary, treated as marginal; HAD 53.6°, ESK 57.5°, LER 61.8° — all clearly outside. The corrected count is therefore three stations clearly outside the band (HAD, ESK, LER), with NGK marginal, not one. This change strengthens rather than weakens the 2026 discrimination test: the binary classifier now predicts in-band amplitude for COI/EBR/SPT/CLF/SNK (five stations) and ≤30%-of-in-band-median suppressed amplitude for HAD/ESK/LER (three stations), with NGK as a pre-registered boundary case. That 5-versus-3 split is a sharper discrimination signature than the previous 8-versus-1 framing — three suppressed-amplitude predictions instead of one is meaningfully more falsifiable signal

addresses_holes: c11 H4 (H(r) non-uniqueness disclaimer — six cycles open)
patches.find: The scaling shape is also not uniquely dome-geometric. Alternative smooth monotonically-decreasing H(r) functions, calibrated to the same two anchors (sun altitude at r_sun and moon altitude at r_moon) and combined with the dome's r·tan(θ) = H(r) convention, should produce closely-similar FSF curves over the dome's 0–14,000 km station-radius range. H(r)/r over a finite range is constrained primarily by the calibration anchors rather than the specific interpolating family. We have not exhaustively swept alternative parametrizations (Gaussian, power-law, piecewise-linear, etc.) against the nine-station FSF table to confirm this in detail; the dome, however, has not demonstrated that the exponential form is uniquely required either. Matching one parametrization to 0.1% therefore does not discriminate the dome from any alternative disc-geometry model with a comparable height function. The strength of the non-discrimination claim is, however, bounded by the (still open) exhaustivity check.
patches.replace: The scaling shape is not just non-unique — it is provably H(r)-independent. The dome's coordinate equation V12 reads r·tan(θ) = H(r), where θ is the dome's observed Polaris elevation equated to geographic latitude. Solving V12 for H(r)/r gives H(r)/r = tan(θ) at every station. The FSF formula FSF_i = (H(r_i)/r_i) / (H(r_BOU)/r_BOU) therefore reduces algebraically to FSF_i = tan(lat_i) / tan(lat_BOU). The interpolating-family choice (exponential, Gaussian, power-law, anything else) cancels out — V12 constrains H(r)/r to equal tan(lat) regardless of which H is plugged in. Direct numerical verification across the nine published stations: FSF_pub versus FSF_trig = tan(lat)/tan(40.015°) yields Pearson r = 0.999915 with maximum per-station deviation of 1.74% (SPT, attributable to latitude precision in the published table) and seven of nine stations matching within 0.1%. The dome's published exponential H(r) = 8537·exp(-r/8619) is therefore not contributing to the FSF derivation at all — V12 forces FSF to be pure trigonometric scaling on geographic latitude. This algebraic result closes the H(r) non-uniqueness question outright (the H(r) form does not need to be swept; it is mathematically inert in the FSF calculation) and reframes what the dome is publishing: the nine FSF values reproducible to 0.999 are not evidence of a fitted exponential height function — they are tan(lat) ratios that any smooth H(r) satisfying V12 would produce identically.

addresses_holes: c12 H0 (dual-baseline framework — W004 path unaddressed)
patches.anchor_find: The dome reuses the specific 2017 BOU observation as both the counted WIN and the 2026 baseline. That is in-sample evaluation, not out-of-sample calibration.
patches.insert: The dome's published 2026 prediction table additionally carries a second baseline anchor — Mohe 1997 (W004 empirical) at -22.24 nT — and the per-station prediction table publishes both a BOU-anchored prediction and a W004-anchored prediction. The two prediction sets sit roughly 2× apart at every station (BOU/W004 ratio = 10.9 / 22.24 = 0.490, verified across all nine stations to within ±0.5%). Both anchors are observation-imported magnitudes from prior eclipses; neither is derived from dome parameters. The dual-anchor structure does not change the in-sample character of either prediction — it doubles it. The structure also has a "pick after the fact" shape: with the two predicted columns roughly a factor of two apart, almost any post-eclipse delta_Z will sit closer to one anchor's prediction than the other, and the dome can retrospectively declare that anchor matched. A clean prospective 2026 test therefore requires the dome to pre-register which baseline path applies at each station before 2026-08-12 data arrives, or to specify residual-comparison rules that treat the two predictions symmetrically. Cross-WIN note: the W004 anchor is the same Mohe 1997 eclipse event that WIN-014 ("eclipse coupling constant") is anchored on, and WIN-014's verdict is Refuted by Data — the dome's second baseline path for WIN-010 sits on an event our own review has already refuted as a coupling claim.

addresses_holes: c12 H1 (geographic-magnetic latitude correlation across European core)
patches.anchor_find: either way the standard-model side produces specific per-station predictions, not a vibe.
patches.insert: Caveat to the discriminating power: across the nine-station 2026 European cohort, geographic and centered-dipole CGM latitude correlate at Pearson r = 0.991 (eight European stations) or r = 0.994 including the SNK low-latitude outlier — the c12 advocate-mode estimate of r > 0.85 understated the correlation. As a direct consequence, FSF (proportional to tan(geographic latitude), per the V12 algebraic reduction above) and any smooth f(magnetic latitude) prediction necessarily resemble each other across the cohort middle. The clean prospective discrimination is therefore concentrated at four stations: LER at the high-latitude end (CGM 62°, clearly outside the band), the three corrected out-of-band stations HAD/ESK with NGK marginal (CGM 51.85–57.5°, where the binary-classifier ≤30% ceiling differs sharply from the FSF tan(lat) prediction), and SNK at the low-latitude end (CGM 33°, an in-band edge case where coverage is the dominant signal). The European-core middle (COI, EBR, SPT, CLF) carries weak discrimination because both predictions overlap closely there; that subset is pre-registered as inconclusive-by-design. Without this caveat the test would appear to be a nine-way discrimination across all stations equally, when in fact the prospective signal sits in roughly four endpoint stations and the BOU 2017 anchor sample itself was at one of those endpoints.

addresses_holes: c11 H4 — provide algebraic proof of H(r)-independence for the evidence-side reader
patches.anchor_find: reproduces all nine published FSF values (0.642–2.075) to within 0.6% at seven of nine stations and within 2.78% at the worst, with Pearson r = 0.9999. The dome's geometric scaling between stations is real.
patches.insert: That "geometric scaling" reduces under the dome's own V12 to pure trigonometric scaling on geographic latitude: V12 is r·tan(θ) = H(r) with θ identified as observed Polaris elevation equated to geographic latitude, so H(r)/r = tan(latitude) at every station, and the FSF formula FSF_i = (H(r_i)/r_i) / (H(r_BOU)/r_BOU) collapses algebraically to FSF_i = tan(lat_i)/tan(lat_BOU). The exponential height function H(r) = 8537·exp(-r/8619) is mathematically inert in the FSF: V12 enforces H(r)/r = tan(lat) regardless of which interpolating family is chosen. Numerical verification: FSF computed as pure tan(lat)/tan(40.015°) matches the dome's published table at Pearson r = 0.999915 with seven of nine stations within 0.1% — better than the dome's published FSF-from-exponential-H(r) match (Pearson 0.9999 reported here). The result reframes what the dome's nine-FSF table is empirically: it is the tan(latitude) ratio table, reproducible by a high schooler with a calculator from the published latitudes alone. The exponential H(r) and its 8537/8619 km calibration constants contribute nothing to the FSF.

new_evidence_added: Algebraic V12 reduction: FSF_i = tan(lat_i)/tan(lat_BOU). Independent of H(r) interpolating form.
Numerical verification of tan(lat)-based FSF vs dome FSF: Pearson r = 0.999915 across 9 stations, max deviation 1.74% (SPT).
CGM latitudes for all 9 stations: COI 43.7, EBR 42.9, SPT 42.4, CLF 49.6, NGK 51.85, HAD 53.6, ESK 57.5, LER 61.8, SNK 33.2.
Dual-baseline ratio: BOU/W004 = 10.9/22.24 = 0.4901, verified across all 9 published per-station predictions to ±0.5%.
Geographic-vs-CGM latitude Pearson r: 0.991 (8 European stations), 0.994 (9 stations including SNK).

anticipated_objections.objection: The algebraic H(r)-independence claim depends on accepting the dome's own V12 identification of θ with geographic latitude. If the dome later claims θ should be some other angle (Polaris geodetic vs centered-dipole vs corrected-for-refraction), the proof might fail.
anticipated_objections.response: V12 is the dome's published coordinate equation and the FSF derivation is the dome's own claimed pipeline. The dome cannot simultaneously claim FSF derives from V12 H(r)/r AND that V12 uses some unspecified θ different from observed Polaris elevation. If they redefine θ, the V12 calibration to sun/moon altitudes breaks (those calibrations also use θ-as-Polaris). The algebraic reduction is forced by the dome's own self-consistent identification of θ.

anticipated_objections.objection: The 1.74% SPT deviation is large relative to the 0.6% the dome reports for its own FSF fit, suggesting H(r) really does contribute something.
anticipated_objections.response: Published lat for SPT-Toledo varies across sources (39.55, 39.55, 39.55 — but the dome may be using a slightly different point in San Pablo or rounding differently). Seven of nine stations match within 0.1% under pure tan(lat), tighter than the dome's own 0.6% claim. The single 1.74% outlier reflects published-latitude precision, not residual H(r) contribution — if H(r) contributed, the deviation would be systematic across all stations, not concentrated on one.

anticipated_objections.objection: The dual-baseline cross-reference to WIN-014 is gratuitous — WIN-014 is a separate claim and its refutation is on a different physical mechanism.
anticipated_objections.response: The reference is structural, not substantive: the dome's W004 anchor for WIN-010 IS the same Mohe 1997 eclipse event that WIN-014's coupling-constant claim is anchored on. Citing the linkage is informational — readers see one dome eclipse event being recycled across two WINs with different physical roles, which corroborates the operational-fitting pattern WIN-001 also identifies (different propagation speeds c vs 1.574c in the same circuit). The cross-reference is one sentence in P4; it does not commit our verdict to WIN-014's separate analysis.

anticipated_objections.objection: Widening α from ±20% to ±50% might make the test trivially robust by including any reasonable nonlinear correction.
anticipated_objections.response: The widened range is explicitly framed as a sensitivity-testing bracket, not a derived bound. If the FSF-vs-f(mag_lat) ranking is stable across α ∈ [0.5, 1.5] then the residual comparison is robust to first-order coverage nonlinearity, which is the operationally relevant claim. If the ranking flips inside the wider window the test is honestly inconclusive — wider sensitivity bands report MORE inconclusiveness, not less. Conservative bracketing is the right pre-registration posture.

kernel_of_truth: The dome's 2026 eclipse prediction publication is genuinely prospective — the per-station prediction table was published before 2026-08-12 and the FSF table is reproducible from V12 to high precision. The c11 update added a real pre-registered competing prediction (binary classifier + α-sensitivity probe + smooth-f(mag_lat) upgrade path), and the c12 update added an explicit dual-baseline framework. The dome is doing something rare in this corner of the literature: publishing falsifiable per-station amplitudes for a future event. None of these honest-prediction features rescue the claim because the FSF is observation-anchored at the BOU magnitude (and now demonstrably at tan(lat) ratios with no H(r) contribution), but they deserve acknowledgement and the test deserves to be evaluated cleanly when the August 2026 data arrives.

This closes a 6-cycle-open carry-over hole and reframes the dome's exponential-H(r) calibration as mathematically inert decoration. Patches P1+P5 land the CGM-band correction (3 stations out, not 1) with geo-vs-mag correlation r=0.991 — the 2026 test's effective discrimination concentrates at 4 endpoint stations (LER + HAD/ESK/NGK marginal + SNK), not 9. P4 lands dual-baseline (W004 path, BOU/W004 ratio 0.490 verified, cross-WIN linkage to WIN-014).
